notes.meaning: David turns to God in deep repentance after the prophet Nathan confronted his adultery. He has nothing to offer God, so he pleads only for God's mercy and loyal love. He asks God to wipe away his record of rebellion, just as someone erases ink from a written scroll.

David asks God to wash him over and over until he is truly clean. Sin is like a deep stain ground into dirty clothes that only hard washing can remove. He knows he cannot cleanse himself and needs God's power to take away his guilt.

David openly confesses what he did wrong instead of making excuses or hiding it. His guilt weighs heavily on his mind and stays before his eyes day and night. Real repentance begins when a person stops making excuses and admits their sin.

David knows he hurt other people, but he sees that all sin is first and foremost an attack against God Himself. Because God is completely holy, any sentence or judgment He gives against the sinner is fair and just.

David looks deep within himself and sees that his evil actions came from a sinful nature he had from his earliest beginning. He does not say this to shift the blame away from himself. Instead, he admits that he was born with a broken human nature that bends toward doing wrong.

God cares about what is on the inside, requiring honesty and pure motives in the deepest parts of the heart. David acknowledges that he cannot produce this kind of goodness on his own. He asks God to teach him true wisdom deep within his soul.

In Israel's worship, priests used a small plant called hyssop to sprinkle water or blood for spiritual cleansing. David asks God to cleanse him spiritually in that same way so that his defilement will be taken away. When God cleanses a sinner, the soul becomes pure and whiter than snow.

David feels crushed in body and spirit under the heavy conviction of his wrongdoing. He asks God to speak words of pardon and peace to his wounded heart. When God forgives, deep sorrow turns into real joy and spiritual healing.

David asks God to turn His eyes away from his offenses and cancel out the debt of his sins. He knows God is holy and cannot look upon evil with approval. When God forgives, He removes our sins from His sight and remembers them no more.

A patched-up heart is not enough, so David asks God for a brand new creation inside him. He needs a steadfast spirit that will stay loyal and not wander back into evil paths. Only God has the power to create a clean heart within a broken person.

David pleads not to be driven out from God's presence or abandoned by His Holy Spirit. He remembers what happened to King Saul and fears losing the guidance and comfort of God's Spirit. He knows that without God's Spirit, he cannot live a life that honors the Lord.

differ.view: New Testament believers should not pray for the Holy Spirit to remain, because Christ promised that the Spirit permanently lives inside every Christian.

notes.meaning: Sin had completely ruined David's inner peace and stolen the happiness of being right with God. He asks the Lord to give that joy back and strengthen him with a willing mind to obey. A glad heart makes obeying God a delight rather than a burden.

Once he experiences God's forgiveness, David promises to help other people who have strayed. He will share what he learned about God's justice and mercy so other sinners will turn back to the Lord. A restored believer can be a helpful guide to others in need of grace.

David specifically confesses the terrible guilt of having Uriah killed. He begs God to deliver him from the penalty and stain of shedding innocent blood. Once he is freed from this burden, his tongue will gladly sing about God's saving mercy.

Guilt, shame, and sorrow had shut David's mouth so he could not worship freely. He asks the Lord to remove this silence by granting him the assurance of forgiveness. When God lifts the heavy burden of guilt, our hearts are freed to praise Him.

The law of Moses provided no animal sacrifices to atone for intentional murder or adultery. Even if such gifts were possible, outward rituals by themselves do not satisfy God. God takes no pleasure in religious ceremonies when the heart is not right with Him.

The offering God truly wants is a heart that is broken and sorry for its sin. A proud person tries to hide wrong actions, but a humble person grieves over offending God. God will never reject or look down on anyone who comes to Him with a truly repentant heart.

David broadens his prayer from his personal needs to include the whole community of God's people. He asks God to show favor to Jerusalem and protect its walls, so that the king's sin will not bring harm to the nation. Good leaders care about the spiritual and physical safety of those they serve.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: These concluding words were likely added during or after the Babylonian exile to pray for the rebuilding of Jerusalem when its walls were broken down.

notes.meaning: When God's people are forgiven and their hearts are right, God takes pleasure in their outward worship. Animal offerings on the altar become meaningful when they flow from genuine devotion. True worship always begins on the inside before it is shown in outward gifts.
